title: What is Exchanger in Java, how do two threads swap objects at a rendezvous point, and how is it used for the double-buffering pattern?

s1_definition.profdef: `Exchanger<V>` is a synchronization point where exactly two threads meet and swap objects. Each thread calls `exchange(myObject)`; the call blocks until the partner also arrives, then each thread receives the object the other brought and both proceed. It is a bidirectional, symmetric handoff for a pair of threads, unlike a queue which is one-directional. The classic use is double buffering: a producer fills a buffer while a consumer drains another, and at the rendezvous they swap, so the producer always has an empty buffer to fill and the consumer always has a full one to process.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture two clerks at National Bank of India standing on either side of a swinging door. The data-entry clerk fills a tray with completed trade forms; the posting clerk empties a tray into the ledger. When both reach the door they swap trays in one motion: the data-entry clerk hands over the full tray and immediately gets back the now-empty one, and the posting clerk does the reverse. Neither waits idle with nothing to do, and no tray is ever touched by both at once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Exchanger is a two-thread rendezvous where each thread hands its object to the other and receives the partner's object in a single atomic swap — perfect for double buffering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Exchanger<V>` is a synchronization point where exactly two threads meet and swap objects. Each thread calls `exchange(myObject)`; the call blocks until the partner also arrives, then each thread receives the object the other brought and both proceed. It is a bidirectional, symmetric handoff for a pair of threads, unlike a queue which is one-directional. The classic use is double buffering: a producer fills a buffer while a consumer drains another, and at the rendezvous they swap, so the producer always has an empty buffer to fill and the consumer always has a full one to process.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture two clerks at National Bank of India standing on either side of a swinging door. The data-entry clerk fills a tray with completed trade forms; the posting clerk empties a tray into the ledger. When both reach the door they swap trays in one motion: the data-entry clerk hands over the full tray and immediately gets back the now-empty one, and the posting clerk does the reverse. Neither waits idle with nothing to do, and no tray is ever touched by both at once.

**One line to remember:** Exchanger is a two-thread rendezvous where each thread hands its object to the other and receives the partner's object in a single atomic swap — perfect for double buffering.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India ingests a stream of settlement trades. A reader thread parses incoming trades into a buffer, and a writer thread posts them to the ledger. If both touch the same list, they corrupt it; if the reader allocates a brand-new list for every batch, the garbage collector thrashes. This is exactly what Exchanger with double buffering solves: the reader fills list A while the writer posts list B, and when the reader's list is full they swap in one atomic motion, so each thread always owns its own list and only two lists ever exist.

Problem 2 — If the reader stalls (upstream feed hangs), the writer must not block forever. The timed `exchange` with a timeout lets the writer give up and raise an alert.

The code builds a `Trade` record, a `TradeReader` that fills a buffer of fixed capacity and swaps at the rendezvous, a `LedgerWriter` that swaps to receive full buffers and posts each trade to update balances for SAV2001 and CUR3001, and a demo that runs both threads and shows the buffers bouncing.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four trades T1..T4, capacity 2, so there are two full swaps.

Step 1: The reader starts with empty buffer A, adds T1 then T2. At size 2 it calls `exchange(A)` and blocks.

Step 2: The writer starts with empty buffer B and calls `exchange(B)`. Now both threads are at the rendezvous, so the swap happens atomically: the reader receives B (empty) and the writer receives A (holding T1, T2).

Step 3: The writer posts T1 and T2 to the ledger, updating SAV2001 and CUR3001 counters, then clears B and calls exchange again. The reader clears A and fills it with T3, T4, then calls exchange again.

Step 4: Second rendezvous: the writer gets the buffer with T3, T4 and posts them; the reader gets the empty one and sends its final partial batch on the last exchange.

Step 5: The writer loop ends after the expected swaps, ledger reports 4 trades posted. Only two list objects ever existed; they just bounced back and forth.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: reader: buffer full, swapping
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: writer: received 2 trades
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Posted T1 amount Rs.50000 to SAV2001
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Posted T2 amount Rs.30000 to CUR3001
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: reader: buffer full, swapping
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: writer: received 2 trades
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Posted T3 amount Rs.20000 to SAV2001
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Posted T4 amount Rs.10000 to CUR3001
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Posted total trades = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Exchanger is a synchronization point where exactly two threads meet and swap objects. Each thread calls exchange with the object it is holding, the call blocks until the partner also arrives, and then both threads get back the object the other one brought. It is symmetric, so there is no sender and no receiver, both sides give and both sides receive in a single atomic handoff.

The textbook use for it is double buffering. I have one thread filling a buffer and another thread draining a buffer, and instead of sharing one list or allocating a fresh list for every batch, I keep exactly two buffers. The filler works on buffer A while the drainer works on buffer B, and when the filler's buffer is full they meet at the exchanger and swap in one motion. The filler walks away with the now-empty buffer and the drainer walks away with the full one. Only two buffers ever exist, so there is no garbage churn, and because exchange establishes a happens-before relationship, everything the filler wrote is safely visible to the drainer without any extra locking.

There is also a timed version of exchange that throws a timeout exception if the partner never shows up, which I use so that a stalled producer cannot block the consumer forever; the consumer simply times out and raises an alert. The one thing to remember is that Exchanger couples exactly two threads, so it is not a broadcast or a general queue. When I want decoupling and buffering I reach for a blocking queue, but when I specifically want a tight paired swap with buffer reuse, Exchanger is the right tool.

At National Bank of India we used this on the trade ingest path. A reader thread parsed incoming settlement trades into one list while a writer thread posted the previous batch to the ledger, and they swapped lists at an exchanger whenever the reader's batch filled up. This kept both threads busy, never shared a list between them, and reused the same two lists for the entire session. The sentence I give interviewers is that Exchanger is a two-thread rendezvous that swaps objects atomically, and its killer application is double buffering where the two buffers simply bounce back and forth between a producer and a consumer.
